data.text/markdown:
04 · Keeping the books

In chapter 03 you worked out the backward steps for Mia's line by hand, then wrote them as code in day_slopes. That works, but only for that one recipe. Change the recipe (a curve instead of a line, a neural network) and you'd have to work out every backward step by hand again. In this chapter you'll build a small engine that does it for you. While a calculation runs, the engine writes down every step in a book, like a shopkeeper keeping the books. Then it reads the book backwards and hands out the blame by itself, using exactly the rules from chapter 03.

What the engine has to do

Recall the rule from chapter 03. Every box gets a blame (how much the loss moves per unit this box moves, for a tiny nudge), and walking backwards:
blame of a box = the sum, over every arrow leaving it, of (local slope of that arrow ||(\times||) blame of the box the arrow points to)
So for every box, the engine must remember three things: its value, the boxes it was made from, and the local slope towards each of them. That calls for a new kind of Python value.

A new kind of value: classes

So far you've used numbers, lists and functions. Python lets you invent your own kind of value, with named slots for whatever it needs to remember. The recipe for a new kind of value is called a class. Think of a form at a doctor's office. The blank form is printed once, with labelled boxes: name, age, phone. Every patient gets their own copy and fills in their own answers. A class is the blank form; each value made from it is one filled-in copy. Our form has four boxes: the number itself, its blame, the boxes it was made from, and the local slopes towards them. Here is the class:

Line by line:
  • class Value: says "here is the recipe for a new kind of value, called Value".
  • def __init__(self, data): is the setup function Python runs every time you make a new Value. The name __init__ (two underscores on each side, short for initialise) is fixed by Python. It has two inputs: self is the new value being set up, and data is the number you give it.
  • self.data = data stores the number in a slot called data, inside this value. A slot like this is called an attribute. The word data appears twice here, meaning two different things: on the left, self.data is the slot inside the value; on the right, data is the input from the def line.
  • self.grad = 0 starts its blame at 0. ("grad" is short for gradient: the blame from chapter 03. It starts at 0 because blame is collected later, by adding.)
  • self.parents = [] and self.local_slopes = [] start as empty lists: the boxes this one was made from, and the local slope towards each, filled in later.
Making one looks like calling a function, but with only one input: Value(3). You never pass self yourself. Value(3) does three things:
  1. Python makes a new, empty value.
  2. It runs __init__, passing that new value in as self and 3 in as data. So self.data = data fills the new value's data slot with 3.
  3. It gives the filled-in value back, and v = Value(3) stores it under the name v.
A dot reads a slot: v.data means "the data slot of v". Each value has its own slots, so below, v and u hold different numbers. (As in chapter 03, several values separated by commas on the last line show up as a numbered list of items, counting from 0.)
Drawn as cards, v and u are two copies of the same form, filled in differently. Their parents lists are empty: nobody worked them out from other boxes, you typed them in.

You can also store into a slot with the dot: v.grad = 5 would replace its blame with 5.

The book

The book is an ordinary list. Every time the engine does one step, it adds the result to the end of the book. Lists have a built-in way to do that: book.append(x) adds x to the end of book. (The dot again: append is a function that belongs to every list.)

One step: multiply

Here is how the engine multiplies two values. It works out the result like normal maths, then fills in the result's memory and writes it in the book:

• out = Value(a.data * b.data): a new box holding the product of the two values.
  • out.parents = [a, b]: it was made from a and b.
  • out.local_slopes = [b.data, a.data]: the local slopes from chapter 03. In ||(a \times b||), nudging ||(a||) moves the result by ||(b||) per unit, and nudging ||(b||) moves it by ||(a||) per unit. The order matches parents: the first slope goes with the first parent.
  • book.append(out): write the step in the book.
  • return out: hand back the new box, so it can be used in the next step.

data.text/markdown:
Reading the book backwards

Now the heart of the engine. After the calculation, the book lists every step in the order it happened, and the last entry is the loss. To hand out blame:
  1. The loss blames itself 1: loss.grad = 1.
  2. Go through the book from the last entry to the first. For each entry, pass blame to each of its parents: add (local slope ||(\times||) this entry's blame) to the parent's blame.
We add to the parent's blame because blames add up when a box feeds several arrows (chapter 03): each arrow out of a box brings its own share. Why from last to first? A box is always written in the book after the boxes it was made from: it can't be worked out before them. So when we read backwards, we reach every box that uses a value before we reach the value itself. By the time we get to a box, all its users have already passed their share of blame to it: its blame is complete, and it's safe to pass it on. Here it is on Mia's day 1 from chapter 03. Recording ||(p = w \times t||), ||(g = p + b||), ||(e = g - s||), ||(L = e \times e||) writes the book in this order: entry 0 is ||(p||), then ||(g||), then ||(e||), then ||(L||). With day 1's numbers, ||(p = 140||), ||(g = 80||), ||(e = 17||) and ||(L = 289||), so the local slope of ||(e \times e||) is ||(2 \times 17 = 34||). Drag the slider to read the book one entry at a time, from the end. The blue outline shows the entry being read; the blames grow under the boxes as they arrive.

Exercise 4: backward

Write backward(loss, book). Your four lines replace todo(), so they all sit inside the def. The first two start at the same place, where todo() was. Each of the last two is pushed in one more step than the line above it, because it sits inside that line's loop. Here is the whole function, so you can see where everything goes: 
def backward(loss, book):
    loss.grad = 1
    for entry in reversed(book):
        for parent, slope in zip(entry.parents, entry.local_slopes):
            parent.grad = parent.grad + slope * entry.grad
Type only the four lines under def: the def line is already there in your cell. It doesn't need to return anything: the blames are stored in the boxes themselves.

Exercise 5: the gradient of the whole loss

Write engine_gradient(w_num, b_num, xs, ys): the slopes of Mia's mean loss for both knobs, computed entirely by the engine. It's chapter 03's gradient, but you only write the forward calculation:
  1. book = [], then the knobs as values: w = Value(w_num) and b = Value(b_num). (w_num is a plain number; w is the box made from it.) From here on, combine boxes only with add, sub, mul and square, never with +, - or *: only those functions write the step in the book.
  2. A running total that is itself a value: total = Value(0).
  3. Loop with for x, y in zip(xs, ys):. Inside: guess = add(mul(w, Value(x), book), b, book), then e = sub(guess, Value(y), book), then total = add(total, square(e, book), book).
  4. After the loop (these lines line up with for, not inside it), the mean is the total times 1 / len(xs): mean = mul(total, Value(1 / len(xs)), book).
  5. backward(mean, book), then return w.grad, b.grad.

The second time, w's blame is 2380, five times 476. On the second pass every box still holds its blame from the first pass, and the new shares are added on top of it, box after box down the book:
  • L is set to 1 again (that line stores, it doesn't add).
  • ||(e||) had 34 and gets ||(34 \times 1||) more: 68.
  • ||(g||) had 34 and gets ||(1 \times 68||) more: 102.
  • ||(p||) had 34 and gets ||(1 \times 102||) more: 136.
  • ||(w||) had 476 and gets ||(14 \times 136 = 1904||) more: 2380.
Each box passes on its whole, already-wrong blame, so the mistake grows at every step. That's why engine_gradient makes fresh Value boxes, with a fresh book, every time it's called: every blame starts at 0. (Real deep-learning tools have the same rule; you'll meet it again later in the course.)

The payoff: a new recipe, no new backward steps

Mia kept selling through a heatwave. Above about 33 °C, sales started to drop: it's too hot to go out. Here are all 11 days:

temps = [14, 17, 20, 22, 25, 28, 31, 33, 35, 37, 39]
sales = [63, 90, 137, 148, 193, 234, 257, 288, 280, 262, 236]

A straight line can't go up and then come down. A curve can:
||[\text{guess} = a \times x \times x + w \times x + b||]
with three knobs a, w and b. With a negative, the curve bends downwards, like a hill. One practical detail: here ||(x||) is the temperature measured from 25 °C, in tens of degrees: x = (t - 25) / 10, so 14 °C becomes -1.1 and 39 °C becomes 1.4. Why? In chapter 02 you saw ||(b||) creep along because the loss reacts more strongly to a knob that gets multiplied by big numbers, so one learning rate was safe for ||(w||) but timid for ||(b||). Here ||(a||) gets multiplied by ||(x \times x||):
||(x||) ||(x \times x||) runs from to
raw temperature ||(t||) ||(14 \times 14 = 196||) ||(39 \times 39 = 1521||)
t / 10 ||(1.4 \times 1.4 = 1.96||) ||(3.9 \times 3.9 = 15.21||)
(t - 25) / 10 0 ||(1.4 \times 1.4 = 1.96||)
With raw temperatures, ||(a||) would be multiplied by numbers up to 1521 and ||(b||) by 1: a learning rate small enough for ||(a||) would leave ||(b||) almost frozen. Dividing by 10 helps, but ||(x \times x||) still reaches 15. Subtracting 25 first puts the middle of the temperatures at 0, so ||(x||) runs from about -1 to 1.5 and ||(x \times x||) from 0 to 2. Now all three knobs are multiplied by numbers of similar size (||(x \times x||), ||(x||), and 1), and one learning rate suits all of them. For a curve, chapter 03 would have meant working out new backward steps by hand. With your engine, you only write the forward recipe. What's next

Your engine handles one number at a time: every multiplication is its own box in the book. Real models work with thousands or millions of numbers at once, and a book entry per number would be far too slow. In Chapter 05 you'll learn to work with whole lists of numbers in one go (vectors and matrices), and then teach the same backward rules to them.

What you can do now

  • define a class with __init__, and read and store attributes with a dot
  • add to a list with append, and walk it backwards with reversed
  • build an engine that records a calculation and backpropagates through it automatically
  • explain why the book must be read backwards, and why each calculation needs fresh boxes
  • fit a new model by writing only its forward recipe
Go deeper (optional): this kind of engine is called automatic differentiation (reverse mode), or autograd. The order we get from the book is a topological order.
